SK1123 Two or alternatives test the same property

x is { A: p } or { A: q } asks one question about one property and spells it as two questions about two objects.

CategoryModernization
Default severityhint
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 9.0
Since2.0

Why

{ A: p or q } is the same predicate with the subject written once, and it is the form the property extends to — a third alternative adds a word rather than a clause. It is also the shape a reader can check: two property patterns side by side have to be compared member by member before it is clear that only the value differs.

Example

Instead of:

if (document is { Status: Draft } or { Status: Review }) {
    Edit(document);
}

Write:

if (document is { Status: Draft or Review }) {
    Edit(document);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The merge is exact and needs no semantic model, because the shape it matches has no type in it. A property pattern with no type resolves its member against the pattern's input type, which is the same input on both sides of an or. Admitting a type — Draft { Status: A } or Review { Status: B } — would be two different members that happen to share a name, so both sides are required to be typeless and the rule stays Syntax. ⚠ The designation guard this rule was written with is refuted, and the compiler is what refutes it. CS8780 — "a variable may not be declared within a 'not' or 'or' pattern" — makes { A: int i } or { A: 2 } and { A: 1 } x or { A: 2 } both uncompilable, confirmed by compiling both, so no program this rule can run on carries a pattern variable there and the guard was unreachable. Its only reachable effect was wrong: a discard is legal under or and merges perfectly well — { A: int _ } or { A: 2 } and its merged { A: int _ or 2 } both compile — so the guard declined a finding it should report. It was removed. ⚠ No parentheses are needed and that is a property of the grammar, not luck. or is the loosest pattern combinator, so a subpattern that is itself an and or a relational run keeps its meaning as an operand of a new or: { A: > 1 and < 5 } or { A: 9 } merges to { A: > 1 and < 5 or 9 }, which still groups the and first. ⚠ Only a plain `Name:` clause. An extended property pattern (A.B: 1) carries a path that may differ between the two sides in ways a name comparison would not see, and merging two different paths is a different predicate. ⚠ A positional clause, more than one subpattern on either side, or two different property names are all declined — each is a shape with no single merged spelling. ⚠ Disjoint from `SK1011` by construction: that rule is registered on && only and its output is a single property pattern with one subpattern and no or, so neither rule can consume the other's result. A comment or a preprocessor directive inside the replaced span withdraws the finding. Generated code is excluded.
